subject: Accounting
title: Overhead Allocation
description: A micro-lesson that makes Overhead Allocation usable.

hook.text: A factory makes chairs and tables. The rent covers both. How do you split it fairly?

buildup.text: Overhead allocation assigns indirect costs to products using a systematic method.

discovery.text: Common methods use machine hours, labor hours, or square footage as the allocation base.

twist.text: The method you choose changes which products look profitable—and that changes business decisions.

climax.text: Activity-based costing offers a more precise approach by tracing overhead to specific activities.

punchline.text: How you split the bill changes who looks expensive.

quiz.question: What is overhead allocation?
options: Assigning indirect costs to products systematically

details.summary: Overhead allocation distributes indirect manufacturing costs—like rent, utilities, and supervision—across products or departments. This topic explains allocation bases, predetermined overhead rates, and why the method chosen significantly affects reported product costs.
details.whyItMatters: Overhead often represents a huge portion of total costs, and there's no single correct way to allocate it. The allocation method chosen directly influences product costs, pricing, and profitability assessments.
takeaways: Predetermined overhead rate equals estimated overhead divided by estimated allocation base
Common allocation bases include direct labor hours, machine hours, and direct labor cost
Over- or under-applied overhead is adjusted at year-end to reflect actual costs

faq.question: How is manufacturing overhead allocated to products?
faq.answer: Companies calculate a predetermined overhead rate by dividing estimated total overhead by an estimated allocation base (like machine hours). Each product then receives overhead based on how much of that allocation base it uses. The rate is set at the start of the year.

faq.question: What happens when overhead is over-applied or under-applied?
faq.answer: Over-applied means more overhead was allocated than actually incurred; under-applied means less was allocated. At year-end, the difference is typically adjusted by debiting or crediting cost of goods sold, correcting the income statement.
